chapter: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
title: Stock arrangements, cut-off titles and the Super Sax Parker transcriptions
summary: Procope explains why titles were cut off stock arrangements, how publishers gave them free to dance bands, published jazz solos, and why Super Sax's five-part Charlie Parker solos were so hard.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Was there much -- were people afraid that others would steal their arrangements? Was there much of that in those days? I remember Elmer Snowden telling me that he used to cut the title off the sheets.
Yeah, they used to do that, but that didn't prove anything. They used to cut the title off because they were all stock arrangements and anybody could go downtown and buy a stock arrangement.

But the thing they used to do downtown, particularly if you were working in dancing schools, we would go down and get about 20 stock arrangements. They'd just give them to you. The publishing companies would just give them to you. You know, you'd tell them you were working in the so-and-so and you'd go downtown and come back with a pile of music, you know. Yeah. Show tunes and dance tunes and jazz tunes which were being published then by -- there was a company in Chicago used to publish the jazz tunes. I can't remember the name, but people used to write, which was supposed to be jazz, I'd say. You know, they were -- well, they were good enough to play, you know, and get ideas from, and some were original and some were not, you know. And then, later on they began publishing Joe Oliver's things that he did in New York when he came to New York. He had some recording dates with Clarence Williams and whatever.
Then they published those things on stock arrangements.
Yeah. Yeah. And then -- it was -- then some of the solos that they published, you know, when you take a jazz solo and write it out.

You know, you've got to be pretty slick to read it, you know, just like I heard this group of saxophone players that were trying to play Charlie Parker's music, his solos. His solos are hard enough to play by themselves, much less harmonize them and play one of Charlie Parker's solos in five-part harmony, that's --

The Super Sax, yes. I heard them in Chicago, and that was pretty rough dealing. And they told me sometimes they'd get through it and sometimes they wouldn't, More than likely more times they didn't, because they weren't meant to be played on the baritone saxophone. How are you going to play Charlie Parker's music on a baritone saxophone. Well, you know, but they attempted it, but it never came off, you know. I don't believe it ever came off, because you never heard it recorded. They couldn't record it. They couldn't record it, no.
